passage: Every morning Papa dropped Siddharth, ten, at the school gate in their car, the radio playing and the AC humming. On Tuesday it poured. From the back seat, Siddharth saw Sumit from his class trudging along the highway's edge, soaked, holding a plastic bag over his books. It was at least three kilometres from the colony Sumit lived in. Siddharth pressed his face to the window. At lunch Sumit's socks were still wet. That evening Siddharth asked, "Papa, why does Sumit have to walk so far and we don't?" Papa put down his phone. "His family doesn't have a car, beta, and there's no school bus from there." "That's not fair," Siddharth said. He felt a strange heaviness, like he'd done something wrong, though he hadn't. "Can we give him a lift when it rains?" Papa thought, then nodded.

qa.q: What did Sumit hold over his books?
qa.a: He held a plastic bag over his books.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he asked Papa about Sumit?
qa.a: Siddharth felt curious and a little guilty, a heaviness as if he'd done something wrong, though he hadn't.

qa.q: What could Siddharth and Papa do next?
qa.a: They could talk to Sumit's family about lifts on rainy days, and Siddharth could keep asking why things are unequal instead of looking away.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel sitting in wet socks at lunch?
qa.a: Sumit probably felt uncomfortable and tired, perhaps embarrassed, after walking so far in the rain.

passage:
"Where do you do your homework?" Bhavna asked, swinging her legs on the school bench.
"On the stairs," said Vinita.
"The stairs?"
"Our room is one room. My brothers watch TV and Dadi prays. So I sit on the stairs outside."
"Isn't it noisy?"
"Neighbours go up and down. But the light is good."
Bhavna thought of her own room: a desk, a lamp, a shelf of books, a door that shut. "I have a desk," she said slowly.
"Lucky."
Bhavna felt her face get warm. "It's not my fault," she said, too fast.
"I didn't say it was."
They were quiet. Then Bhavna asked, "Why is it like that?"
Vinita shrugged. "Some people have more rooms."
"Do you want to do homework at my house on Saturday?"
Vinita smiled. "Okay."

qa.q: Where does Vinita do her homework?
qa.a: She does it on the stairs.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna say "It's not my fault" too fast?
qa.a: Bhavna felt guilty and a bit defensive after realising how different their homes were.

qa.q: What small step did Bhavna take, and why is it kind?
qa.a: Bhavna invited Vinita to do homework at Bhavna's house, sharing a quiet space instead of feeling guilty alone.

qa.q: How does Vinita seem to see the difference?
qa.a: Vinita seems matter-of-fact, saying "Some people have more rooms," without blaming Bhavna.

grounding: A child learns a friend studies on noisy stairs while the child has a desk, and starts to ask why, feeling guilty, curious and a little defensive.

passage: I was twelve when I first really noticed. I'd go to the corner shop at night for milk, and there was Abhinav, from my class, sitting on the step under the street lamp, doing his maths homework. Every night. I had my own room and a table lamp. One night I asked him why he didn't study at home. "Power cut in our lane," he said. "Again." I walked home feeling weird. I thought: I got ninety in maths and he got seventy-five, and everyone called me clever. But he was doing sums under a street lamp with mosquitoes biting. I felt guilty, then annoyed at feeling guilty, then just curious. Why was our lane always lit? Next week I asked my teacher. She explained about the old wiring in some areas. I'm Jomon, and that was the first time I wondered who gets what, and why.

qa.q: Where did Abhinav do his maths homework?
qa.a: He sat on the step under the street lamp.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel walking home that night?
qa.a: Jomon felt guilty, then annoyed at feeling guilty, then curious about why things were so unequal.

qa.q: What did Jomon do with the curiosity, and why was it useful?
qa.a: Jomon asked a teacher about it, which turned an uncomfortable feeling into understanding about unequal starting points.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see his nightly studying?
qa.a: Abhinav seems to accept it as normal, simply explaining the power cut, perhaps not expecting anyone to notice.

grounding: A child notices a classmate studying under a street lamp and starts asking why their starting points differ, feeling guilty and curious.

passage: Thomas, you asked on the podcast about a time I got defensive. Okay. Last month in class, we were talking about the board results. Rani said, "Well, Devika had tuition for three subjects and her own laptop. Of course she topped." I felt my face go hot. I snapped, "I worked really hard! I studied every night!" Everyone went quiet. I was so angry. I felt like she'd erased all my effort. But later, at home, looking at my laptop, I thought about Rani. She shares one phone with two sisters for online classes. She still got eighty-five. So both things were true. I worked hard. And I had a lot of help she didn't have. Saying the second doesn't cancel the first. I'm Devika, and I still wince remembering how I snapped.

qa.q: How many subjects did Devika have tuition for?
qa.a: Devika had tuition for three subjects.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when Rani spoke about tuition?
qa.a: Devika felt attacked and angry, as if Devika's effort had been erased.

qa.q: What did Devika realise later, and why does it matter?
qa.a: That hard work and unearned advantages can both be true, and admitting the second does not cancel the first.

qa.q: How might Rani have felt when Devika snapped?
qa.a: Rani may have felt frustrated and unheard, since she was pointing out a real difference in resources.

grounding: A teenager told of having it easier feels attacked and insists on hard work, then sees that effort and advantage can both be true.

passage:
Monday: In the canteen, Pooja said, "Manoj got into the science olympiad team because his father's a professor. He had all those books at home." Manoj slammed his tray down. "I worked for it! I did every past paper!" Pooja shrugged. Manoj stormed off, furious.
Wednesday: At home, Manoj looked at his father's shelves: rows of science books, a microscope, old olympiad papers. He remembered Pooja telling him once that she studied from borrowed textbooks with missing pages. He still felt stung.
Saturday: Manoj found Pooja in the library. "I did work hard," he said. "But you're right, I had stuff you didn't. Both are true." Pooja looked surprised. "That's all I meant." He pushed a stack of old papers across. "Want these?"

passage: Abhinav, you're angry because your friend said you had it easy? Let me tell you about me at sixteen. I'm your Vijay chacha. I topped the district in class ten. Our neighbour's son, Ramu, said at the celebration, "Of course he did. He had a tutor, a quiet room, and he never had to work in the fields." I was so angry I threw my sweets on the ground. I had worked! I woke at five! How dare he? For years I told that story as proof people were jealous. Only when I became a teacher and saw children studying after long days in the fields did I understand Ramu. Both things were true: I worked hard, and I had help he never got. Admitting the help didn't make my work smaller. It just made me more honest.

passage: In the Delhi University canteen, Rajni, twenty, listened to her classmates plan their summers: an internship through someone's uncle, a coaching class in Mumbai, a trip abroad "to build the CV." Zeenat, her friend, said, "What about you?" Rajni shrugged. "Tuition job. Same as last year." Her father drove an auto in Meerut. She'd studied in a Hindi-medium government school, learnt English from newspapers, and got here through an entrance exam she'd prepared for alone. Listening to them, she felt a sour resentment rise. They'd started the race ten steps ahead and didn't even know it. Then Zeenat said, "You know you topped the stats midterm, right? Without any coaching." Rajni blinked. She did know. The resentment didn't vanish. But beside it, something steadier appeared: pride in how far she'd come.

qa.q: What does Rajni's father do?
qa.a: Her father drove an auto in Meerut.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling as her classmates planned their summers?
qa.a: Rajni felt a sour resentment, knowing they had started far ahead without realising it, and later a steadier pride.

qa.q: How did Zeenat's comment help Rajni?
qa.a: Zeenat reminded Rajni of topping the midterm without coaching, which helped her feel pride alongside the resentment.

qa.q: How might Rajni's classmates see their summer plans?
qa.a: They likely see them as normal and earned, unaware of the head start their connections and money give them.

grounding: A student from a modest background sees peers with connections and coaching, feels the race began at different lines, and holds resentment alongside pride.

passage:
"You're not going to the Goa trip?" Harsha asked, scrolling on his phone.
"Can't," said Tanvir. "Have to send money home this month."
"Oh. Ask your dad?"
"My dad's a watchman, Harsha."
Harsha looked up. "Sorry. I didn't think."
"It's fine." Tanvir stirred his tea. "Most people here don't think. You all had coaching, laptops, uncles who know people. I learnt coding on a cyber café computer."
"That's... actually really impressive."
"It's also really tiring." Tanvir laughed, but it came out tight. "Sometimes I'm angry. Like I'm running with a bag of bricks and everyone's cheering the guys with sneakers."
Harsha was quiet. "And sometimes?"
"Sometimes I look at where I started and think, look how far I got." He shrugged. "Both."

passage: My roommate in first year, Sangeeta, was lovely. But I noticed things. When she failed a subject, her parents paid for a private tutor within a week. When her laptop broke, a new one arrived the next day. Her father called a friend, and she had an internship in second year. When my scholarship payment was delayed, I skipped meals for a month and didn't tell anyone. When my phone cracked, I used it cracked for two years. Some nights I lay awake, bitter. It felt like we were running the same race but she had started halfway down the track. I didn't hate her. I just felt invisible. Now, in final year, I'm the first in my family to reach a degree. I'm Binita, and when I think of that, the bitterness shares space with a fierce pride.

qa.a: Binita used it cracked for two years.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling on those sleepless nights?

passage:

Vidya didn't feel like a saint, and she didn't pretend she'd got her job on her own. She just tried to share the doors she happened to stand beside.

passage: Hansa, you asked why I always forward job openings to so many people. Let me tell you. I'm Hafsa, your mother's old friend. When I was twenty-four, my father knew half the city's editors. I got my first newspaper job with one phone call. I was proud, and also ashamed, because I knew girls who wrote better than me and had no one to call. For a while I pretended I'd got it on merit alone. Then I met Shobha, from a small town, brilliant, stuck proofreading. I didn't give up my job; that wouldn't help her. Instead I showed her work to my editor and asked him to read it without knowing her background. He hired her. After that I made a habit: every opening I hear of, I pass on widely. I don't carry guilt like a sack. I just try to open the doors I can.

qa.q: How did Hafsa get the first newspaper job?
qa.a: Hafsa got it with one phone call.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling about getting the job that way?
qa.a: Hafsa felt proud and ashamed at once, knowing others wrote better but had no one to call.

qa.q: Why was showing Shobha's work to the editor a turning point in Hafsa's story?
qa.a: It turned Hafsa's advantage into an opportunity for someone else, instead of either denying the head start or wallowing in guilt.

qa.q: How might Shobha have felt when she was hired?
qa.a: Shobha likely felt relieved and recognised, finally judged on her writing.

grounding: An elder recalls recognising a head start through family connections and using it to share opportunities fairly, without guilt or denial.

passage: The hiring deadline was midnight, the office Wi-Fi kept dropping, and Madhav, twenty-six, was the only one on the team who could recommend candidates for the new analyst role. His cousin had sent a CV that morning: decent, but not the best. Madhav knew he had grown up with English at home, a father in the industry and an easy route in. He also knew Usha, from the evening data course he taught, was sharper than anyone. She'd studied in a small-town college and had no one to put in a word. Madhav felt the pull to help family. He also felt the old guilt about his own easy route. He set both aside and wrote a fair recommendation for Usha, listing her work. Then he called his cousin and suggested two other openings. passage: In class five, I spent more time looking at Kamal's paper than my own. When the teacher returned tests, I'd peep at his mark first. If I'd beaten him, I felt ten feet tall. If he'd beaten me, I felt tiny, even if I'd got eighty-five. I did the same with drawings, sports day ribbons, even how many stars we got in our notebooks. It helped a bit: I knew where I stood, and I worked harder in maths because of him. But slowly, I stopped enjoying anything unless I'd won. One day, Kamal got a prize for a poem, and I felt sick, although I didn't even like writing poems. My mother asked why I was sad. I couldn't explain. I'm Nazia, and looking back, I'd tied my whole mood to a boy who didn't even know I was counting.

qa.q: What prize did Kamal get?
qa.a: Kamal got a prize for a poem.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel when Kamal beat Nazia in a test?
qa.a: Nazia felt tiny and deflated, even after scoring well, because the comparison set the mood.

qa.q: What could help Nazia keep the useful side of comparing?
qa.a: Nazia could use comparison to learn, like working harder in maths, while also noticing personal progress and enjoying tasks for their own sake.

qa.q: How might Kamal have seen their class five year?
qa.a: Kamal probably didn't know Nazia was counting and just got on with his own work.

grounding: A child looks back on checking a classmate's marks and prizes, feeling proud or small by ranking, and seeing how constant comparison coloured self-worth.

Kiran (class four) has started checking everyone's drawings before starting their own. Today, when Vaibhav held up a bright elephant, Kiran looked at their own sketch, crumpled it and said, "Mine's rubbish." Last week, when Kiran's painting was put on the board above Vaibhav's, Kiran grinned all day and told everyone. Comparing seems to help Kiran see what good work looks like, but it's starting to decide how Kiran feels about everything. I sat with Kiran and asked what they liked about their own drawing before it was crumpled. Kiran said, "The trees." I suggested keeping a folder of their drawings so they can see their own progress over the year. We'll start tomorrow.

Sports day. I got a silver in the sack race and a bronze in the relay. I was SO happy. Then I saw Yash had three golds. Three! Suddenly my medals looked like tin.
In class I always check his marks too. If I'm higher, I feel like a queen. If he's higher, I don't want to eat my tiffin.

I don't know. Maybe because he's there and last year's me isn't.
I put the silver on my shelf anyway. It's still shiny.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Monday.
Manjula (class ten) came in today, low and teary. She said she spends two hours every night scrolling through classmates' pages. Pooja's especially: holidays in the hills, trophies, perfect family dinners. "My life is so boring. I'm behind at everything," she said. When I asked what she'd done that week, she listed a science project, helping her Nani, and a funny afternoon with her cousins. She hadn't counted any of it. We talked about how pages show the best moments, not the ordinary ones. She laughed a little when I asked if Pooja posted her bad hair days. We agreed she'll try muting a few accounts for a week and write down one good thing each night. Follow-up next Monday.

qa.q: How long does Manjula spend scrolling every night?
qa.a: She spends two hours every night scrolling through classmates' pages.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when she said her life was boring?
qa.a: Manjula felt low and behind, as if everyone else's life was brighter than hers.

qa.q: Why is writing down one good thing each night a helpful step?
qa.a: It helps Manjula notice her own ordinary good moments, instead of comparing them to others' highlights.

qa.q: How might Pooja's life look different offline?
qa.a: Pooja probably has boring and bad days too; her page just shows the best moments.

grounding: A teenager scrolling classmates' polished pages feels dull and behind, forgetting she only sees highlights, and a counsellor helps her notice her own days.

passage:
Thursday night
Scrolled for an hour again. Sunaina went to a concert in Mumbai, then posted a photo with her new guitar, then her science fair trophy. Everyone commented fire emojis and "queen."
I spent today doing algebra and eating rajma in my room.

Divyansh reacted differently. He asked Arvind how he'd prepared, made a list of skills to learn, and started practising two hours every evening. "If Arvind did it, I can too," he said. Watching him, I realised the same news had pushed him forward and pulled me down. The difference was that he saw the goal as reachable. I didn't. Later, I asked Divyansh to show me his list.

passage: When I was nine, everyone at home called me "slow Rekha." Slow to eat, slow to dress, slow at sums. My cousin Noor, who lived with us, was "clever Noor." When a hard puzzle came in the newspaper, Papa gave it to Noor. When a guest asked a question, they looked at her. After a while, I stopped trying the hard sums at all. Why bother? I was the slow one. I'd just wait for Noor. And Noor, being called clever, tried everything, even things she didn't know yet. In class six, a new teacher gave me a hard problem and said, "I think you can do this." I stared at it for twenty minutes and got it right. I remember my hands shaking. I'm Rekha, and I sometimes wonder how many years that label cost me.

qa.a: Expecting Rekha to succeed gave Rekha the push to try, showing how others' beliefs shape what children attempt.

Mridul (class four) has been called "the lazy one" by several teachers since class two, and he now says it about himself: "I'm lazy, ma'am, I won't finish." Today he didn't even start the maths worksheet. Payal, who is often called "the clever one," asked for an extra hard sheet. Both children seem to be living up to what they've heard. I sat with Mridul and asked him to do only the first three sums with me. He did them correctly and quickly. I told him, "That wasn't lazy. That was careful and fast." He looked surprised. qa.a: Payal seems encouraged to take on harder tasks, confident because others expect success.
